Talk about a birth and a newborn baby.
It's 14 December, two o'clock at night. Mara is on the night shift. Her phone rings: it's Jonas, from the second floor of the hospital, from the delivery room.
Mara! Mara, are you awake? It's starting! Clara has had contractions since ten. The midwife says it won't be long now!
Jonas, I'm on the night shift, of course I'm awake. Where are you?
In the delivery room, second floor. Can you come? Clara wants to see you. She says you're the only nurse she trusts.
I'll ask my colleague if he can take over the ward for ten minutes. Breathe deeply, Jonas.
Me? I don't have to breathe. Clara has to breathe!
You both have to breathe. I'm coming.
Mara… It's a boy! A little boy! He's here! At seventeen minutes past two!
I'll be with you right away! How's Clara? And the boy?
They're both fine. He weighs three thousand four hundred grams. He has red hair, like his mother. And he screams like his father, Clara says.
And do you already have a name for the little one?
Yes. But we'll tell you the name when you're here. In person. It's a surprise.
“KRICE-zahl”: ei = “eye”, ß = s, aa = long a.
“HAYP-ah-me”: the b is devoiced (sounds like p) after the long e.
A group of MASCULINE nouns take the ending -(e)n in every case except the nominative singular:
der Junge, der Kollege, der Kunde, der Löwe, der Neffe
der Rumäne, der Pole, der Türke, der Franzose
der Student, der Patient, der Praktikant, der Polizist, der Soldat
der Mensch, der Herr (den Herrn), der Nachbar (den Nachbarn), der Bär
“der Name” is special: den Namen, dem Namen, but des NAMENS (-ns in the genitive). The same goes for “der Gedanke” (the thought).
On envelopes and in letters: “Herrn Ludwig Brandt” (accusative / dative). “Sehr geehrter Herr Brandt” (nominative, when addressing someone).
Many German nouns are formed from verbs or adjectives. The suffix tells you the gender:
hoffen → die Hoffnung, wohnen → die Wohnung, erfahren → die Erfahrung
frei → die Freiheit, gesund → die Gesundheit, krank → die Krankheit
möglich → die Möglichkeit, freundlich → die Freundlichkeit
Freund → die Freundschaft, Nachbar → die Nachbarschaft

Mara ran down the stairs, two steps at a time, even though she always told the nurses you mustn't run in a hospital. Her colleague Emil, a young trainee doctor from Leipzig, had taken over the ward after she had promised to make him coffee for a whole week.

In the delivery room it was quiet and warm. The light was soft. Clara was sitting in bed, her red hair spread over the pillow, her face tired and happy at the same time. On her chest lay a tiny human being in a white cloth, with red hair and tightly closed eyes, making soft little sounds, like a kitten. Jonas was standing by the bed and crying without realising it.
Mara. Come here. I want to introduce you to someone.

Mara went over to the bed. She had seen many newborns in her life, hundreds, in Sibiu and in Berlin. But this boy was different. This boy was her friends' son, the boy whose godmother she was going to be, the boy whose parents she had met one New Year's Eve, when the father had burnt his hand and the mother had found a ring in her glove.
Mara, this is Ludwig. Ludwig Andrei Weber.
Mara looked at the two of them. Then at the little boy. Then at the two of them again. She couldn't say anything.

Ludwig, because without his suit our wedding would only have been half as beautiful. And because he's the best person we know. And Andrei, because… well. Because he's our godmother's brother. And because Lena said that otherwise she won't sell us any more cakes.

Mara was laughing and crying at the same time. The midwife, an older woman with short grey hair, who had worked in this delivery room for thirty years and had already seen everything, handed her a tissue and said drily: “Nurses don't cry at work, Ms Ionescu.” Then she took a second tissue for herself too.
At six in the morning, when Mara's shift was over, she called Ludwig. She knew that at this hour he was already up, with Fritz, with his first coffee, under the yellow lamp.
Ludwig? The baby's come. A boy. Healthy and loud. And they've given him a name. Maybe you should sit down.

When she told him the name, there was silence at the other end for a long time. So long that Mara thought the line had been cut off. Then she heard a sound she didn't recognise at first. Ludwig was blowing his nose. Loudly. Twice.
The dust. There's so much dust here, Mara. In this old flat.

Within an hour the whole of Kastanienallee knew. Instead of the usual pretzels, Lena baked small bread rolls in the shape of baby bootees and gave them to every customer who could say “Congratulations”. Andrei, who was just leaving the bakery, heard the news on the stairs and stopped in the middle of a step. “Andrei? The middle name is Andrei?” He immediately called his mother in Sibiu, who immediately told all the neighbours, so that two hours later half of Sibiu knew that a little boy with her son's name had been born in Berlin. Kuba and Ola painted a big picture of a baby, a tram and two dogs that looked like sausages, and hung it on the front door. Underneath, in colourful letters, it said: “Welcome, little Ludwig! From your neighbours, whom you don't know yet.”

Three days later, Clara, Jonas and little Ludwig came home to their flat in Friedrichshain. On the first Sunday, big Ludwig went to see them on the M10, in his grey suit, with a parcel under his arm. In it was a small yellow wooden tram, which he had built and painted himself over the last three nights. On the side, in tiny letters, was the number 5218.

He held the little boy for a long time in his big old hands, carefully, as if he were made of glass. The boy opened his eyes, which still had the dark colour of all newborns, and looked at him. Seriously and curiously, like a little person seeing the world for the first time. Ludwig whispered something in his ear. Nobody heard what. But Clara said later that the boy smiled for the first time at that moment. The midwife would have said that newborns can't smile yet at that age. But the midwife wasn't there.

On the way back, on the tram, Ludwig called Mara. “Do you know what I told him?” he asked. Mara didn't know. “I told him: welcome, little person. You've chosen a good family. And a very good godmother. Don't give them any worries. And learn early on how to brake.”

Mara laughed. Then she asked him what he was going to do now, on a Sunday afternoon in December, alone on the tram. Ludwig didn't answer straight away. Outside, the houses of Friedrichshain went by, the lights of the Christmas markets, people with bags and red hats. “You know,” he said at last, “I think I'll just ride to the end of the line and back. Once right through the whole city. I haven't done that for a long time. Just to see how beautiful it's become.” Mara said it was a very good idea. And that she'd wait for him with dinner.

In the evening, Mara sat with Mrs Hoffmann on the fourth floor and told her everything. The old pianist listened without interrupting and smiled the whole time. When Mara had finished, she stood up, slowly, as always, and went to the piano. “For little Ludwig,” she said. Then she played a lullaby by Brahms, very softly, with the window open, even though it was December and cold. Down in the courtyard, under the bare chestnut tree, a young man with flour in his hair stopped and listened. On the first floor a window opened under a yellow lamp. And on the second floor, two children pressed their noses against the glass, with an old dog between them, and forgot for five minutes that they should really have been asleep already.
